# Regular expression built from HTTP request data (Node.js)

`qualor:js/regex-injection` · Issue · Severity: Medium · [CWE-1333](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1333.html), [CWE-400](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
HTTP request data used as the pattern of a regular expression: `new RegExp(x)` or `RegExp(x)`
(Express, Fastify, Next.js, Node's `http`). Request data as the text that a constant pattern is
tested against, and the flags argument, are fine and not reported.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
JavaScript's regular expression engine backtracks. A crafted pattern such as `(a+)+$` can take
exponential time on a short input, and since Node.js runs requests on a single event loop, one such
request stalls every other request (ReDoS). A pattern from the client can also simply match more
than intended, for example `.*` where one name was meant.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the search term is used as a pattern.

```javascript
const express = require('express');

const app = express();
const names = ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'];

app.get('/search', (req, res) => {
  const pattern = new RegExp(req.query.q, 'i');
  res.json(names.filter((n) => pattern.test(n)));
});
```

**Compliant:** the term is escaped (lodash `escapeRegExp()`), so it matches only itself.

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const { escapeRegExp } = require('lodash');

const app = express();
const names = ['alice', 'bob', 'carol'];

app.get('/search', (req, res) => {
  const pattern = new RegExp(escapeRegExp(req.query.q), 'i');
  res.json(names.filter((n) => pattern.test(n)));
});
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Escape request text before building a pattern: `RegExp.escape()` (ES2025), lodash
  `escapeRegExp()` or the `escape-string-regexp` package.
- For plain substring search, skip regular expressions: `value.includes(term)`.
- Or pick the pattern from a fixed allow-list, or test request data against a constant pattern
  (`/^[a-z]+$/.test(value)`).
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- Express
- Next.js
- Fastify
- Node.js http
- Lodash
- escape-string-regexp

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- `text.match(x)`, `text.matchAll(x)` and `text.search(x)`, which turn a string into a pattern,
  are not checked, and neither is MongoDB's `$regex` operator.
- A pattern first validated by a constant pattern and a value stripped down to letters and digits
  are still reported.
- Hand-written escaping is recognised in its common form only:
  `value.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')` (also `replaceAll`), whose character class holds
  every syntax character `^ $ \ . * + ? ( ) [ ] { } |`, written in place or in a helper of the
  same file that only returns it and is declared before the call. An escape that misses a
  character or the `g` flag is reported, as it should be; a helper declared after the call, a
  replacement function, a pattern kept in a constant and helpers of other modules are reported
  too. MDN advises `RegExp.escape()` over hand-written escaping.
- An allow-list check is recognised only as an early `return` or `throw` after `includes()` or
  `has()` on a constant list of string literals; the same check as the condition of an `if` around
  the use is not. The check covers the value up to its next assignment; an assignment inside a
  nested block after the check (`if (x) { q = req.query.other; }`) or a destructuring assignment
  (`[q] = [req.query.other]`) is not seen, so the value is still taken for checked.
- An element of a request array reached through a callback
  (`req.body.filters.map((f) => new RegExp(f.pattern))`) is missed.
- Results of awaited calls on other objects (a database lookup by a request value) are taken for
  stored data. When a function is passed to such a call (`await cache.wrap(key, async () =>
  ...)`), only the value of the call is; a pattern built inside the callback is checked as usual.
- Request handlers are recognised by the name of their second parameter (`res`, `reply`, `ctx`,
  `next`, ...): a handler written as `(request, out)` is not checked.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test files [`rules/js/regex/regex-injection.js`](../../../rules/js/regex/regex-injection.js) and [`rules/js/regex/regex-injection.ts`](../../../rules/js/regex/regex-injection.ts) hold every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/js/regex/regex-injection.yml`](../../../rules/js/regex/regex-injection.yml), added in version 2026.10.1.
